Fuel Planning in Remote Britain

Running out of fuel is more than an inconvenience when you're touring the UK — in some areas, it's a genuine safety concern. Large stretches of the Scottish Highlands, mid-Wales, and northern England have fuel station gaps of 40-60 miles. For bikes with smaller tanks or thirsty engines, that margin gets uncomfortably tight. Here's how to plan ahead and keep riding.

The UK's Fuel Deserts

Understanding where fuel is scarce is half the battle. These are the key areas where stations are widely spaced:

  • Northwest Highlands: Between Ullapool and Durness, stations are 40+ miles apart. The NC500 route is spectacular but fuel-sparse.
  • Central Highlands: The A9 corridor has stations, but venture off it towards Torridon or Knoydart and you're in fuel-desert territory.
  • Mid-Wales: Between Machynlleth and Brecon, the mountain roads are fantastic but fuel stations are rare. Plan your fill-ups around the A470 corridor.
  • North Pennines: The A686 and surrounding roads are some of England's best biking territory, but fuel options thin out between Penrith and Hexham.
  • Scottish Borders: The rolling hills hide sparse infrastructure. Fill up in towns like Hawick, Jedburgh, or Kelso.

Know Your Bike's Real Range

Your bike's theoretical range and its actual touring range are very different things. Loaded with luggage, riding into a headwind, on hilly terrain, and at varying speeds, fuel consumption increases significantly.

  • Calculate your actual mpg by filling up, riding a known distance, and filling up again. Do this loaded, in real conditions.
  • Use 80% of your theoretical range as your safe planning distance.
  • A bike with a 15-litre tank averaging 50mpg has a theoretical range of 165 miles — plan for refuelling at 130 miles maximum.
The rule we follow at VisorUp: never pass a fuel station in a remote area with less than half a tank. Even if it means a 5-minute stop you didn't plan. The security is worth it.

Fuel Station Types and Hours

Not all fuel stations are equal in rural Britain:

  • Supermarket stations: Cheapest, but only in larger towns. Open long hours.
  • Branded stations (BP, Shell, Esso): Mid-price, reliable. Often 6am-10pm in rural areas.
  • Independent rural stations: Lifesavers in remote areas. May close at 6pm, may not open Sundays, may be cash-only. Don't rely on assumed opening hours — check in advance.
  • Pay-at-pump 24hr: Increasingly common but still rare in the most remote areas. Require a card with a PIN.

Fuel Planning Tools

Several tools can help you plan fuel stops into your route:

  • Google Maps: Search "petrol station" along your route. Shows opening hours and reviews.
  • PetrolPrices.com: UK fuel station locator with prices and opening hours.
  • VisorUp route planner: Our built-in fuel overlay shows station density along your planned route.
  • OS Maps: Marks fuel stations on detailed maps — useful for offline planning.

Emergency Fuel Measures

If the worst happens and you're running critically low:

  • Switch to reserve (if your bike has a reserve tap) or watch your fuel gauge carefully.
  • Ride at a steady 50-55mph in a high gear to maximise economy.
  • Avoid heavy acceleration and unnecessary engine braking.
  • In the Highlands, farm vehicles and local drivers may be able to spare a litre — don't be afraid to ask politely.
  • As an absolute last resort, breakdown cover will bring fuel to you, but response times in remote areas can be hours.

Fuel planning takes five minutes at the start of each day and prevents the one problem that will definitely end your riding day prematurely. Make it a habit, and you'll never need to worry. faq.q: How far apart are fuel stations on the NC500?
faq.a: On the northwest Highland section between Ullapool and Durness, stations can be 40 or more miles apart. The NC500 is spectacular but genuinely fuel-sparse, so fill up in Ullapool and Durness and never assume the next village will have a pump. Mid-Wales, the North Pennines and the Scottish Borders are similarly thin.

faq.q: How do I work out my bike's real touring range?
faq.a: Fill up, ride a known distance loaded and in real conditions, then fill up again to calculate your actual mpg. Loaded, into a headwind and over hilly terrain, consumption rises significantly. Use 80% of your theoretical range as your safe planning distance. A 15-litre tank at 50mpg gives 165 theoretical miles, so plan to refuel by 130.

faq.q: What is the golden rule for remote fuel?
faq.a: Never pass a fuel station in a remote area with less than half a tank, even if it means a five-minute stop you did not plan. In fuel-desert country the security is worth far more than the time saved, because the alternative is a recovery that can take hours to reach you.

faq.q: Are rural fuel stations always open?
faq.a: No. Supermarket stations in larger towns are cheapest and open long hours, but independent rural stations can close at 6pm, not open on Sundays, and sometimes only take cash. Do not rely on assumed opening hours; check in advance using Google Maps or PetrolPrices.com, both of which show hours and locations.

faq.q: What should I do if I am running critically low?
faq.a: Switch to reserve if your bike has a tap, then ride at a steady 50 to 55mph in a high gear to maximise economy, avoiding heavy acceleration and unnecessary engine braking. In the Highlands, local drivers or farmers may spare a litre if you ask politely. As a last resort, breakdown cover will bring fuel, though response times in remote areas can be hours.
